outcome: Judged: the status rests on bound-level progress — Klartag's April 2025 n²·2^-n lattice lower bound, alongside AI-produced upper-bound work (Huawei/UCL, Astra) of the same tier; nothing settles the bullet. [Judged 2026-09-28; the researcher's original outcome follows.] The general-dimension asymptotic sphere packing problem remains open, but several distinct results moved bounds since January 2024: Klartag (Apr 2025) proved a new lattice lower bound of order n²·2^-n (up from the Campos–Jenssen–Michelen–Sahasrabudhe n·log n·2^-n bound of Dec 2023, which itself predates the frozen revision); a Huawei Noah's Ark/UCL team (Dec 2025) used a Bayesian-optimization + Monte Carlo Tree Search pipeline to find new state-of-the-art upper bounds for dimensions 4-16 via the Cohn–Elkies three-point method; and OpenAI's internal 'Astra' model (Aug 2026) is claimed to have determined the exact asymptotic exponent of the Cohn–Elkies linear-programming bound, capping what that method can ever achieve — the first improvement to the general high-dimensional upper-bound exponent since 1978. None of the problem's core open question (the true asymptotic packing density in general dimension) has been resolved; the densest classification is 'claimed' because the most significant single result (Astra's Cohn-Elkies exponent) is Lean-verified and has an informal mathematician digestion (Seewoo Lee) but has not cleared traditional peer review, and is under an active, unresolved priority/attribution dispute.

ai.basis_quote: Astra works on the problem, sometimes for a long time, and produces the core insight and strategy for a proof; human mathematicians then write that strategy up as a traditional, readable manuscript, and the model translates the manuscript into the strict formal syntax of Lean.
ai.disclosed_cost: OpenAI reported that finding all ten proofs (including this one) cost the equivalent of roughly $2,000 in AI usage fees, a figure that omits the cost of unsuccessful attempts and is not broken out per problem.

disputes.summary: Steven Miller (Yeshiva University) says Astra's sphere-packing (Cohn–Elkies exponent) proof reuses an argument from his own 2016 paper without adequate attribution; a similar unattributed-prior-work complaint was raised by Fournier-Facio (Cambridge) about a different one of the ten results (nonsofic groups). OpenAI's response: 'We take responsibility for the correctness of these results and are meeting the same standards generally expected of human mathematicians.' As of six weeks after release (per Scientific American, published in the Sept 2026 window), the dispute is unresolved and none of the ten results has cleared traditional peer review.

summary: Three separate, unrelated developments touch this bullet's asymptotic sphere-packing-density question since 26 January 2024, and none of them settles the general problem. (1) Boaz Klartag (arXiv:2504.05042, submitted 2025-04-07, v2 2026-01-25) proved a new lattice sphere-packing lower bound of order c·n²·2^-n via a 'stochastically evolving ellipsoid' construction, a quadratic-in-n improvement over the previous best construction (Campos–Jenssen–Michelen–Sahasrabudhe, arXiv:2312.10026, Dec 2023 — which itself predates the frozen revision and is not counted as an in-window event, though it is the baseline Klartag improves on). Gil Kalai's blog (2025-04-09) calls it 'an amazing breakthrough'; a Lean formalization of Klartag's result also appears to exist (per an issue on the leanprover/lean-eval-submissions repo), giving this piece close to 'resolved'-level digestion, though it is only a lower-bound improvement, not a resolution — classified as `progress` in isolation. No AI system produced this mathematics; it is pure human work by Klartag. (2) A Huawei Noah's Ark / UCL AI Centre team (arXiv:2512.04829, submitted 2025-12-04) used a Bayesian-optimization-plus-Monte-Carlo-Tree-Search pipeline to search for polynomial pairs in the Cohn–Elkies three-point semidefinite-programming method, reporting new state-of-the-art upper bounds on packing density for dimensions 4-16 (excluding 8). This is `ai_role: bound` in isolation — an AI system moved a numerical upper bound on a still-open problem, not a proof. (3) The most significant event, and the one this record's top-level fields describe, is OpenAI's internal 'Astra' model (announced 2026-08-01, in a 249-page manuscript plus Lean 4 certificates), which is claimed to have determined the *exact* asymptotic growth rate of the Cohn–Elkies linear-programming bound itself (exponent √(e/2π) ≈ matching an exponent decay rate), the first improvement to the general high-dimensional sphere-packing upper-bound exponent since 1978. This caps what the Cohn–Elkies method can ever prove, but is not itself a resolution of the sphere-packing problem (it supplies no new packing and does not pin down the true asymptotic density) — mathematically this is best read as `progress`/`claimed` on the upper-bound side rather than a full resolution. Authors' own account (via secondary reporting, since the primary PDF could not be parsed by the fetch tool) describes a pipeline where Astra 'produces the core insight and strategy for a proof,' humans write it up, and the model formalizes it in Lean — squarely `ai_role: generated` under §6.2, since the mathematics in the result originated from the model rather than from checking/proofreading a human argument. As of six weeks post-announcement, the claim has an informal mathematician digestion (Seewoo Lee spent two weeks reconstructing and explaining the proof, though his post explicitly says he does not yet understand how the upper- and lower-bound exponents match) but no traditional peer review, and is under an active, unresolved priority dispute with Steven Miller over uncredited prior work. This combination — Lean-checked, informally digested, not peer-reviewed, disputed — is exactly the profile of `claimed` rather than `resolved`. I also checked and excluded DeepMind's AlphaEvolve result (new kissing-number lower bound in dimension 11, 592→593, announced 2025) as out of scope: the kissing number problem is a related-but-distinct problem from sphere-packing density, with its own separate Wikipedia bullet, so under §3.1 it is a related problem rather than a case of this one.
competing_reading: One could argue the overall record should be `progress` rather than `claimed`, on the view that the Astra result, however striking, is an upper bound on a bounding *method* rather than the packing problem itself, so the strongest single move is really Klartag's `progress`-level lower bound. I chose `claimed` because it is the most classification-relevant status the frozen bullet's asymptotic behavior has seen: the Cohn–Elkies exponent result is a genuine mathematical resolution of a sub-question (the ultimate power of the linear-programming method), it is the event with an actual (if incomplete) AI-authorship claim requiring adjudication under §6.2, and `claimed` still correctly signals 'not yet settled by peer review' rather than overclaiming `resolved`.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a completed peer-reviewed publication or widely-accepted expert consensus (e.g., a second independent 'digestion' post or a journal referee report) on the Astra Cohn–Elkies exponent result, resolving the Miller priority dispute one way or the other, or (b) a genuine resolution of the asymptotic sphere-packing density itself (as opposed to a bound on a bounding method), which remains fully open.
